analysis.one_liner: Strips greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide out of the Clean Air Act, ending EPA climate regulation.
analysis.headline: The bill to exempt greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act attracted 154 cosponsors but died in committee without ever getting a vote in the 111th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Clean Air Act's definition of "air pollutant" to exclude carbon dioxide, methane, water vapor, and other greenhouse gases, and would declare that nothing in the Act can be used to regulate climate change [S2] [S3]. In practice, it would bar the EPA from using its existing Clean Air Act authority to limit the emissions driving global warming, leaving power plants, oil refineries, and other large emitters free of federal climate rules [S2]. It was introduced nine days into the new Congress and never received a hearing or vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Large emitters of greenhouse gases — coal-burning power plants, oil and gas companies, and energy-intensive manufacturers — gain if the bill passes, because the EPA would be permanently barred from limiting their carbon emissions under the Clean Air Act. Companies would avoid compliance costs, and the prospect of future carbon limits would be taken off the table by statute.

how_it_helps.text: The bill excludes carbon dioxide, water vapor, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, and sulfur hexafluoride from the Clean Air Act's definition of "air pollutant" [S3].

It further declares that nothing in the Clean Air Act authorizes or requires the regulation of climate change or global warming, foreclosing EPA action even through other provisions of the Act [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the costs: the emissions the bill exempts are the principal drivers of climate change, and the public would face the resulting harms — more severe heat, storms, and sea-level rise — plus any continued local air pollution from the facilities that escape federal oversight. Taxpayers and households would eventually absorb the costs of climate damage that regulation was designed to limit.

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove the main existing legal tool for limiting U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, leaving no federal backstop as climate effects worsen [S2] [S3].

Supporters argued that EPA regulation of carbon under rules written for smog and soot was an ill-fitted and costly way to handle climate policy, and that such a consequential decision should rest with Congress rather than agency regulators — a fair-faith objection even if the bill's cure was to prohibit any regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers no offsetting public benefit for the climate costs it locks in. It does not create an alternative climate policy; it simply prohibits the one that exists. Whatever the genuine concerns about EPA overreach, the bill's effect is a one-way transfer of risk from large emitters to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Energy and Environment Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on January 9, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce that same day [S1] [S5].
On January 14, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Environment, where no further committee action occurred [S5].

On July 23, 2009, Blackburn filed a motion to discharge the committee from further consideration (Discharge Petition No. 111-5) — a device to force a bill out of committee — but the petition did not produce a floor vote [S5].
The bill attracted 154 cosponsors, including 152 House Republicans and 2 House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the public kept the Clean Air Act's existing framework for addressing greenhouse gases, which the EPA went on to use. Large emitters lost the chance to have their exemption from climate regulation written into statute, and House leadership never had to schedule a vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, which kept existing climate authority

for.name: Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and later filed a discharge petition (Petition 111-5) to try to force it out of committee and onto the floor.

for.name: 152 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to exempt greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction (Chair Henry Waxman, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Environment Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup during the Congress; even a discharge petition filed in July 2009 did not move the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily one-sided: 152 of 178 House Republicans cosponsored, versus just 2 of 253 House Democrats, and the committee that buried it was run by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently exempted their carbon emissions from Clean Air Act limits, avoiding compliance costs. The public would bear the resulting climate and air quality harm instead.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Emissions from oil and gas operations would be beyond EPA climate regulation, shielding the industry from carbon rules and future liability.
Facilities with large greenhouse gas emissions would escape federal climate requirements, shifting those costs onto the public.
The bill would strip the agency of authority over greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act, removing the main existing federal tool for limiting emissions that harm the public.
